questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Three point charges are fixed on a straight line: P (+7 μC) at x = 0, Q (+5 μC) at x = 0.3 m and R (+3 μC) at x = 0.6 m. Take 1/(4πε0) = 9 × 10^9 N m² C^-2. The net electric force on Q is:
questions.explanation: The force of P on Q is 9 × 10^9 × (7 × 10^-6)(5 × 10^-6)/(0.3)² = 3.5 N, repulsive, so it pushes Q towards R. The force of R on Q is 9 × 10^9 × (3 × 10^-6)(5 × 10^-6)/(0.3)² = 1.5 N, repulsive, so it pushes Q towards P. The pushes oppose, so the net is 3.5 - 1.5 = 2.0 N towards R. Adding the magnitudes to get 5.0 N forgets the opposite directions.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 1 Electric Charges and Fields: Coulomb's law and the superposition principle for forces on a charge

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: An infinite plane sheet carries a uniform surface charge density of 1.77 × 10^-7 C m^-2. Take ε0 = 8.85 × 10^-12 C² N^-1 m^-2. The electric field at a point 5 cm from the sheet is:
questions.explanation: Gauss's theorem gives E = σ/(2ε0) for an infinite plane sheet, independent of the distance from it. E = 1.77 × 10^-7/(2 × 8.85 × 10^-12) = 1.77 × 10^-7/(1.77 × 10^-11) = 1 × 10^4 N C^-1. The value σ/ε0 = 2 × 10^4 N C^-1 belongs to the field just outside a charged conductor, and dividing by the 5 cm distance wrongly makes the field fall off.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 1 Electric Charges and Fields: Gauss's theorem applied to a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: An electric dipole of moment 8 × 10^-7 C m is placed in a uniform electric field of 5 × 10^5 N C^-1 with its axis at 30° to the field. The magnitude of the torque on the dipole is:
questions.explanation: The torque on a dipole is τ = pE sinθ = 8 × 10^-7 × 5 × 10^5 × sin 30° = 0.40 × 0.5 = 0.20 N m. Using cos 30° in place of sin 30° gives 0.35 N m, and dropping the angle factor gives 0.40 N m, which is the maximum torque at 90°.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 1 Electric Charges and Fields: torque on an electric dipole in a uniform electric field

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A thin spherical shell of radius 25 cm carries a uniform charge of +16 μC. A point charge of −6 μC is fixed at the centre of the shell. Take 1/(4πε0) = 9 × 10^9 N m² C^-2. The magnitude of the net electric field at a point 15 cm from the centre is:
questions.explanation: The field of a uniformly charged thin shell is zero at every point inside it, so only the point charge at the centre contributes. E = 9 × 10^9 × 6 × 10^-6/(0.15)² = 2.4 × 10^6 N C^-1. Using the net charge of +10 μC gives 4.0 × 10^6 N C^-1, which wrongly treats the shell's charge as sitting at the centre for an interior point.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 1 Electric Charges and Fields: Gauss's theorem and the field inside a uniformly charged thin spherical shell

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about electric fields.
(A) Electrostatic field lines do not form closed loops.
(B) The tangent to a field line at a point gives the direction of the force on a negative test charge placed there.
(C) The net force on an electric dipole placed in a uniform electric field is zero.
(D) Closer field lines in a region indicate a stronger electric field there.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
questions.explanation: Field lines begin on positive charges and end on negative ones, so electrostatic field lines never close on themselves. A uniform field pulls the two charges of a dipole with equal and opposite forces, so the net force is zero, and a crowded line pattern marks a strong field. The tangent gives the force direction on a positive test charge; a negative charge is pushed the opposite way, so that statement is false.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 1 Electric Charges and Fields: properties of electric field lines and a dipole in a uniform field

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A body carries a net charge of −4.8 × 10^-18 C. Take the charge of an electron as 1.6 × 10^-19 C. The number of excess electrons on the body is:
questions.explanation: Charge is quantised, so Q = ne and n = |Q|/e = 4.8 × 10^-18/(1.6 × 10^-19) = 30. The negative sign shows that the body has gained electrons. An answer of 3 comes from treating 10^-18/10^-19 as 1 instead of 10.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 1 Electric Charges and Fields: quantisation of charge, Q = ne

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A charge of +4 μC and a charge of −1 μC are fixed 50 cm apart. At what distance from the +4 μC charge, on the line joining them and between the two charges, is the electric potential zero?
questions.explanation: Potential is a scalar, so the two contributions simply add: k(4 μC)/x − k(1 μC)/(0.5 − x) = 0 gives 4(0.5 − x) = x, so x = 0.4 m = 40 cm. At that point 4/0.4 = 1/0.1 in the same units. The midpoint (25 cm) is wrong because the charges differ, and 33.3 cm comes from applying the inverse-square condition that belongs to fields.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 2 Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance: potential due to a system of point charges

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: An electric dipole of moment 2 × 10^-8 C m is held in a uniform electric field of 5 × 10^4 N C^-1 at an angle of 60° to the field. Taking the potential energy to be zero when the dipole is perpendicular to the field, its potential energy is:
questions.explanation: For a dipole at angle θ to the field, U = −pE cosθ. Here pE = 2 × 10^-8 × 5 × 10^4 = 1 × 10^-3 J, so U = −1 × 10^-3 × cos 60° = −5 × 10^-4 J. Using sin 60° gives −8.7 × 10^-4 J, which is the torque-type factor, and −1 × 10^-3 J is the value at θ = 0.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 2 Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance: potential energy of an electric dipole in an external field

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A parallel plate capacitor with plate separation 8 mm has a capacitance of 5 pF in air. A dielectric slab of thickness 4 mm and dielectric constant 4 is then introduced between the plates, parallel to them. The new capacitance is:
questions.explanation: With a slab of thickness t and constant K, the effective gap is (d − t) + t/K = 4 + 1 = 5 mm, so C = C0 × 8/5 = 5 × 8/5 = 8 pF. Treating the slab as a conductor (gap d − t = 4 mm) would give 10 pF, and 20 pF (K × C0) would hold only if the dielectric filled the whole gap.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 2 Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance: capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor with a dielectric slab

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem:
Arrange the following modifications of a parallel plate capacitor of capacitance C0 in increasing order of the capacitance obtained.
(A) Plate area halved
(B) Plate separation doubled and the gap filled with a dielectric of constant 3
(C) Plate separation tripled
(D) Plate area doubled and plate separation halved
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
questions.explanation: Capacitance varies as KA/d. The four values are: area halved, 0.5 C0; separation doubled with K = 3, 3/2 = 1.5 C0; separation tripled, C0/3; area doubled with separation halved, 2 × 2 = 4 C0. In increasing order these are C0/3, 0.5 C0, 1.5 C0 and 4 C0. Ranking the separation-tripled case above the area-halved case is the usual slip, since 1/3 is smaller than 1/2.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 2 Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance: parallel plate capacitance C = Kε0A/d

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Free electrons in a metal wire drift at 9 mm s^-1 when the electric field in the wire is 1.5 V m^-1. The mobility of the electrons, in m² V^-1 s^-1, is:
questions.explanation: Mobility is the drift speed per unit electric field, μ = vd/E. Converting 9 mm s^-1 to 9 × 10^-3 m s^-1 gives μ = 9 × 10^-3/1.5 = 6.0 × 10^-3 m² V^-1 s^-1. Leaving the speed in millimetres gives 6.0, a slip of the unit prefix, and multiplying the speed by the field instead of dividing gives 1.4 × 10^-2.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 3 Current Electricity: drift velocity and mobility, μ = vd/E

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: A uniform wire of resistance 4 Ω is stretched uniformly to three times its original length, with its volume unchanged. Its new resistance is:
questions.explanation: At constant volume the cross-sectional area falls by the same factor by which the length rises. With L → 3L and A → A/3, R = ρL/A becomes 9 times larger, so R' = 9 × 4 = 36 Ω. Using R ∝ L alone gives 12 Ω, which forgets that the cross-section also shrinks.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 3 Current Electricity: resistance R = ρL/A of a wire stretched at constant volume

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Four identical cells, each of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 1 Ω, are connected in parallel across an external resistor of 2.75 Ω. The current through the resistor is:
questions.explanation: Identical cells in parallel give the emf of a single cell, 1.5 V, with internal resistance r/n = 1/4 = 0.25 Ω. The current is I = 1.5/(2.75 + 0.25) = 0.50 A. Using the full 1 Ω of a single cell gives 0.40 A, which ignores how the parallel cells share the current.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 3 Current Electricity: combination of cells in parallel and internal resistance

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Kirchhoff's junction rule and loop rule respectively express the conservation of:
questions.explanation: The junction rule states that the total current entering a junction equals the total leaving it, which expresses conservation of charge. The loop rule states that the algebraic sum of potential changes around a closed loop is zero, which expresses conservation of energy. Swapping the two gives the reversed pairing, a common slip.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 3 Current Electricity: Kirchhoff's junction rule and loop rule

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: In a Wheatstone bridge PQRS the arms have resistances PQ = 10 Ω, QR = 20 Ω, PS = 15 Ω and SR = 30 Ω. A galvanometer of resistance 100 Ω joins Q and S, and a battery is connected between P and R. The equivalent resistance between P and R is:
questions.explanation: The ratio 10/20 equals 15/30, so the bridge is balanced and no current flows through the galvanometer, whose resistance is therefore irrelevant. The paths P-Q-R and P-S-R are 30 Ω and 45 Ω in parallel: 30 × 45/75 = 18 Ω. Adding all four arms in series gives 75 Ω, and counting only one path gives 30 Ω.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 3 Current Electricity: Wheatstone bridge, balance condition and equivalent resistance

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Two bulbs rated 60 W, 120 V and 40 W, 120 V are connected in series across a 120 V supply. The total power drawn from the supply is:
questions.explanation: From R = V²/P the resistances are 120²/60 = 240 Ω and 120²/40 = 360 Ω. In series the total is 600 Ω, so the power drawn is V²/R = 14400/600 = 24 W. Adding the ratings gives 100 W, which is wrong because each bulb now receives less than its rated voltage; 9.6 W is only the power in the 60 W bulb (0.2² × 240).
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 3 Current Electricity: electrical power P = V²/R for bulbs in series

questions.subject: physics
questions.stem: Match List-I with List-II. List-I: (A) Resistivity (B) Conductivity (C) Mobility of charge carriers (D) Current density. List-II: (I) A m^-2 (II) m² V^-1 s^-1 (III) Ω m (IV) Ω^-1 m^-1. Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
questions.explanation: Resistivity has the unit Ω m and conductivity, its reciprocal, has Ω^-1 m^-1. Mobility is the drift speed per unit field, so its unit is m² V^-1 s^-1, and current density is current per unit area, A m^-2. Interchanging resistivity and conductivity is the common slip, since one is the reciprocal of the other.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 3 Current Electricity: resistivity, conductivity, mobility and current density with their SI units

questions.subject: physics
questions.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.stem: A short bar magnet has a magnetic moment of 2 A m². Take μ0/4π = 10^-7 T m A^-1. The magnetic field at a point on its axis, 10 cm from its centre, is:
questions.explanation: On the axis of a short bar magnet, B = (μ0/4π) × 2m/r³ = 10^-7 × 2 × 2/(0.1)³ = 4 × 10^-4 T. The equatorial field is half of this, (μ0/4π) × m/r³ = 2 × 10^-4 T, which is also what results from leaving out the factor 2. Using r² in place of r³ gives 4 × 10^-5 T.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 5 Magnetism and Matter: magnetic field on the axis of a bar magnet

questions.subject: physics
questions.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.stem: Match List-I with List-II. List-I: (A) Bismuth (B) Aluminium (C) Soft iron (D) Alnico. List-II: (I) Paramagnetic (II) Ferromagnetic, low coercivity, used in electromagnet cores (III) Diamagnetic (IV) Ferromagnetic, high coercivity, used in permanent magnets. Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
questions.explanation: Bismuth is diamagnetic and aluminium is paramagnetic. Soft iron has low coercivity and retentivity, so it makes a good electromagnet core, while alnico has high coercivity and retentivity and is used for permanent magnets. Pairing soft iron with permanent magnets is the usual slip, since both are ferromagnetic.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 5 Magnetism and Matter: dia-, para- and ferromagnetic substances with examples, soft and hard ferromagnets

questions.subject: physics
questions.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.stem: The magnetic susceptibility of a paramagnetic sample is 2 × 10^-5 at 300 K. At what temperature will its susceptibility be 4 × 10^-5, if Curie's law holds?
questions.explanation: Curie's law gives χ = C/T, so the susceptibility is inversely proportional to the absolute temperature. For χ to double, T must halve: 300 K becomes 150 K (check: 2 × 10^-5 × 300 = 4 × 10^-5 × 150 = 6 × 10^-3). Taking χ directly proportional to T gives 600 K, the common slip.
questions.ncert_ref: NCERT Class 12 Physics Part I, Ch 5 Magnetism and Matter: Curie's law and the effect of temperature on paramagnetic susceptibility
